summary:
The Sac and Fox Nation is a self-governing nation based near Stroud, in central Oklahoma. Most of its citizens descend from the Thakiwaki, or Sauk, people, and the Nation's language department works with elders to keep the Sauk language spoken.

The name "Sac and Fox" is a federal label. It does not describe a single people. In an 1804 treaty, the United States combined the Sauk with the Meskwaki, whom the French called the Fox. The two peoples are close relatives in language and culture, but they have stayed politically separate.

The Thakiwaki homelands lay in the western Great Lakes. Treaties and armed conflict later pushed the people from Illinois to Iowa, then to a reservation in Kansas, and finally to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. The Black Hawk War of 1832 broke out after the Sauk lost their town of Saukenuk in Illinois. It ended with soldiers killing unarmed people as they tried to cross the Mississippi River.

Children at the Sac and Fox Agency School were punished for speaking their language, and the loss was felt for several generations. Today the Nation has an elected government, its own tribal court and language programs. The Olympian Jim Thorpe was Sac and Fox, and his Olympic rings appear on the Nation's seal and flag.

notes: Word count is about 205. Two sources back each date: 1804 (OHS and Iowa PBS) and 1832 (OHS, NPS and meskwaki.org). LEFT OUT: (1) The year of the move to Indian Territory. OHS says Kansas 1847–1867 and Indian Territory 'in the 1870s', but the Missouri nation's site places the removal in 1869. These conflict. (2) The 1867 reservation size (about 480,000 acres) and the 1867 treaty. Only OHS gives them. (3) The Sac and Fox Mission School dates, 1872–1917. Only the Nation's own site gives them. (4) The OHS population figure (about 3,000 in Oklahoma). There is one source and it may be out of date. (5) The Nation's 'first' to take on IHS self-governance. It has one source and is a superlative. Saukenuk is sourced to OHS plus Illinois tourism. The Nation's own website has almost no narrative history. Its About page covers culture and language only, so most of this history rests on OHS. TravelOK repeats OHS word for word, so it is not counted as an independent source. The Jim Thorpe seal and flag detail has one source (OHS). The fact that he was a member has two (OHS and NPS).
